music.0: paata is the song, paadu is to sing: same pair as Tamil paattu and paadu.
music.27: baagundi is the word you will hear most in Hyderabad: food, music, a shirt, all baagundi.

numbers.0: okati: OK, a tea. One OK cup of tea.
numbers.14: enni (how many) and entha (how much): enni for things you count, entha for money and size.

questions.0: Almost every Telugu question word starts with e: enti, ekkada, eppudu, enduku, entha, enni, evaru.

describe.0: Add di to the describing word and it becomes the whole sentence: pedda, peddadi (it is a big one).

rules.title: The verb goes last
rules.body: Who, then what, then the action. The action word closes the sentence, exactly like Kannada and Tamil.
rules.example: nenu roju piano vaayistaanu = I play the piano every day.

rules.title: The ending tells you who
rules.body: Telugu sticks the person onto the end of the verb: aanu for I, aavu for you (a friend), aaru for polite you and for they, aadu for he, undi for she, aamu for we. You can even drop nenu or nuvvu, the ending already says it.
rules.example: vaayistaanu (I play), vaayistaavu (you play), vaayistaadu (he plays), vaayistaamu (we play).

rules.title: She and it share an ending
rules.body: In the singular, Telugu grammar puts women in the same group as things, so she and it take the same ending: undi now, indi in the past. It is only grammar and nobody hears it as rude. To show respect to an older woman, use the polite aaru ending instead.
rules.example: aame vaayistundi (she plays), athanu vaayistaadu (he plays). aame vaayinchindi (she played). Respectful: aavida vaayistaaru.

rules.title: A wish and a skill sit with the person
rules.body: For want, need and know how to, the person takes ki or ku (naaku, meeku) instead of being the plain subject.
rules.example: naaku chai kaavaali (I want tea), naaku vaayinchadam vachchu (I know how to play), naaku vaayinchaalani undi (I want to play).

rules.title: No word for is
rules.body: To say what something is, put this and the thing side by side. For is not, add kaadu at the end.
rules.example: idi maamidi pandu = this is a mango. idi maamidi pandu kaadu = this is not a mango.

rules.title: Polite meeru and andi
rules.body: With elders, strangers and shopkeepers use meeru, and end a request with andi. andi also softens yes and no: avunandi, ledandi.
rules.example: meeru vastaaraa? (are you coming?) raandi, koorchondi (please come, please sit).

rules.title: Questions end in aa
rules.body: Stretch the last sound into aa and the statement becomes a yes or no question. Nothing else moves.
rules.example: nuvvu piano vaayistaavu (you play the piano). nuvvu piano vaayistaavaa? (do you play the piano?) tinnaavaa? (did you eat?)

rules.title: ki for to, lo for in
rules.body: ki or ku means to, lo means in or at, nunchi means from. They stick on the end of the place, and English words take them too.
rules.example: intiki (to home), office ki (to the office), Hyderabad lo (in Hyderabad), Hyderabad nunchi (from Hyderabad).

commandNote: Polite ends in andi (vaayinchandi, raandi, ivvandi); a friend or a child gets the short form (vaayinchu, raa, ivvu). Do not: verb plus aku, or akandi to be polite (vaayinchaku, vaayinchakandi).
